English

Etymology 1

From Middle English han, contraction of haven.

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /hæn/, /heɪn/
    • Audio (Southern England):(file)
    • Audio (Southern England):(file)
  • (unstressed) IPA(key): /hən/
  • Rhymes: -æn, -eɪn

Verb

han

  1. (obsolete) plural simple present of have
    • 1579, Edmund Spenser, The Shepheardes Calender:
      They han the fleece, and eke the flesh;
    • 1614, William Browne, The Shepheards Pipe:
      Since that ye han had my virginitie,
    • 1748, James Thomson, The Castle of Indolence: […], London: […] A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC:
      And his alluring Baits suspected han.
    • 1976, “Howfen Wakes” (track 1), in Howfen Wakes‎, performed by The Houghton Weavers:
      Ee lads 'an ya fowt? Nay, we'n not fowt yet.

Central Franconian

Alternative forms

  • hann (most dialects)

Etymology

    From Middle High German hān, from Old High German havēn, northern variant of habēn, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan.

    Pronunciation

    • IPA(key): /hɑn/, [ɦɑn]

    Verb

    han (irregular, third-person singular present hat, past tense hauw, past participle jehad, past subjunctive häu)

    1. (Ripuarian and Kölsch, auxiliary, with a past participle) to have (forms the perfect and past perfect tense)
    2. (same dialects, transitive) to have; to own (to possess, have ownership of; to possess a certain characteristic)
    3. (same dialects, transitive) to have; to hold (to contain within itself/oneself)
      Uur hat doa Floep va.
      You are afraid of that.
      (literally, “You have fear of that.”)
    4. (same dialects, transitive) to have, get (to obtain, acquire)
    5. (same dialects, transitive) to get (to receive)
    6. (same dialects, transitive) to have (to be afflicted with, suffer from)
    7. (same dialects, transitive, of units of measure) to contain, be composed of, equal
      Ing Menuut hat 60 Sekonde.
      There are 60 seconds in one minute.
      (literally, “One minute has 60 seconds.”)
    8. (same dialects, impersonal, with het or 't) there be, there is, there are
    9. (same dialects, with 't and mit) to be occupied with, to like, to be into
      Iech han't nit zoeë mit Höng.
      I'm not a great fan of dogs.
      (literally, “I don't have it that much with dogs.”)
    10. (same dialects, with 't and uvver) to talk about
      Vier hauwe't juus uvver dienge Vrunk.
      We were just talking about your friend.
      (literally, “We just had it about your friend.”)

        Middle Norwegian

        Alternative forms

        • hann

        Etymology

        Inherited from Old Norse hann, earlier *hánn, from Proto-Norse *ᚺᚨᚾᚨᛉ (*hanaʀ /⁠hānaʀ⁠/), of uncertain origin.

        Pronoun

        han

        1. he (third-person nominative and accusative singular masculine personal pronoun)
          wi haffuum fore gudz sculd oc fore donda manna bøn sculd vpgeffuit med vælborin man Nissa Knwtzson all the brot som han haffuer moti os brotit till thenne dagh for then sculd at han er waar man oc waar thienare wordin meder so skelom at han gøre malseghandomen lika fore theirra scada oc vppa thet at han vore os thes ytter meir till thienesto
          We have for Gods sake and by request of honourable men, pardoned the wellborn man Nisse Knutsson for all the violations he has committed against us to this day, because he is become our man and servant, provided he makes amends with the representatives for their damages so that he may continue to be of service to us.
        2. it (third-person nominative and accusative singular masculine non-personal pronoun)
          sagde Haluarder thetta er myn elgher. Nicolis sagde ney. sagde tha Haluarder er elghan saar a vinstre sidhonne tha er han myn. tha vende their ælghen vm oc skodhadho oc fans ther saret sem Haluarder sagde. tha swaradhe Nicolis er han thin tha fla han. en flaar thu thenna ælgh aldri scaltu fla ælghen oftare.
          Halvard said: "this is my elk". Nicolas denied it. Halvard then said: "if the elk has a wound on its left side then it is mine". They flipped the elk onto its other side, and saw and found the wound that Halvard had mentioned. Then Nicolis responded: "if it is yours then flay it, but were you to flay this elk you shall never again flay another".

        Norwegian Bokmål

        Norwegian Wikipedia has an article on:
        Pronomen
        Wikipedia no

        Pronunciation

        • IPA(key): /han/, [hanː]
        • Rhymes: -an
        • Homophones: hann, hand
        • Hyphenation: han

        Etymology 1

        Inherited from Middle Norwegian han, from Old Norse hann, from Proto-Norse *ᚺᚨᚾᚨᛉ (*hanaʀ /⁠hānaʀ⁠/), of uncertain further origin. Proposed explanations include a demonstrative related to Ancient Greek κεῖνος (keînos, “that one”) and a formation from a pronominal stem related to English he.

        Cognate with Danish han, Swedish han, Icelandic hann, Faroese hann and Norn hann (“he”).

        Pronoun

        han (objective han or ham, possessive hans, plural de)

        1. he; the third-person masculine singular personal pronoun, referring to a male person.
          Han er broren min. ― He is my brother.
          • 1930, “Dommernes bok”, in Bibelen‎, 6:21:
            Herrens engel rakte ut staven han hadde i hånden
            The angel of the Lord stretched out the staff he was holding.
          • 1874, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt‎, page 222:
            se, det fik fanden, fordi han var dum
            See, that is what the devil got for being stupid.
          • 1875, Henrik Ibsen, Digte‎, page 107:
            kongen han bygged dagen lang
            The king, he built all day long.
          • 1892, Henrik Ibsen, Bygmester Solness‎, page 8:
            Deres søn, han blir naturligvis her hos mig
            Your son, he will naturally stay here with me.
          • 1874, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt‎, page 12:
            hvor er skæpperne med mynt efter gamle Rasmus Gynt? Faer din gav dem fødder, han
            Where are the bushels of coins left by old Rasmus Gynt? Your father made them disappear, he did.
          • 1884, Henrik Ibsen, Vildanden‎, page 83:
            han ser nu så kleint, far Deres
            Your father does have poor eyesight now.
          • 1884, Henrik Ibsen, Vildanden‎, page 206:
            Gregers: «Hvor kan De tænke Dem, at en personlighed som Hjalmar –?» – Relling: «Å, personlighed – han!»
            Gregers: “How can you imagine that a personality like Hjalmar—?” Relling: “Oh, a personality—him!”
          • 1873, Henrik Ibsen, Kærlighedens komedie‎, page 25:
            hun blev ham og han blev hende tro
            She remained faithful to him, and he to her.
          • 1925, Herman Wildenvey, Fiken av Tistler‎, page 131:
            og gaar du paa gaten en dag med en herre, saa hviskes det ogsaa i klynger og klikker: Det er noget galt med ham der og han derre
            And if one day you walk down the street with a gentleman, people whisper in their little groups and cliques: There is something wrong with those two.
          • 1988, Arild Nyquist, Giacomettis forunderlige reise‎, page 74:
            selv hadde han ikke sovet et eneste minutt, og var dødssliten etter alle strabasene
            He himself had not slept a single minute and was exhausted after all the exertion.
          1. he; referring to a male animal.
            Hunden heter Max. Han er tre år gammel. ― The dog's name is Max. He is three years old.
            • 1874, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt‎, page 9:
              [rypesteggen] flaksed kaglende, forskræmt, fra den knart, hvor han sad gemt
              [The male ptarmigan] fluttered away, cackling in fright, from the rocky knoll where he had been hiding.
            • 1895, Henrik Ibsen, Lille Eyolf‎, page 34:
              Mopsemand, han svømmer bagefter
              Mopsemand, he swims along behind.

          1. (colloquial) that, this; stressed before a male name or noun, suggesting unfamiliarity or distance.
            Hvem er han Per du stadig snakker om? ― Who is this Per you keep talking about?
            • 1918, Halfdan Kjerulf, Av hans efterladte papirer 1847–1868‎, page 250:

              That fellow at the newspaper may come out with something.

              I asked whether you are still together with that Philip?
        8. (dated or humorous) you; addressing a man, formerly from a social superior to an inferior, often condescendingly.
          Vil han komme hit med en gang! ― Will you come here at once!
          • 1853, Henrik Wergeland, Samlede Skrifter‎, volume III, page 486:

            “What do you mean by that? What is being said about the house?” the consul asked sharply.
        9. (dialectal) it; referring to the weather or sea conditions, including as an impersonal subject.
          Han er kald i dag. ― It is cold today.

            Look how it is clouding over; thunder and lightning are coming.

            krap og brydsom sjø … vi er i et strømras, hvor han gaar tverket
            A choppy, troublesome sea […] we are in a tidal race where it runs crosswise.
          • 1896, Thomas Krag, Ada Wilde‎, page 252:
            idag er han fin for skogfuglen
            Today the weather is good for hunting woodland grouse.
          • 1922, Nils Kjær, Samlede skrifter‎, volume IV, page 68:
            han blaaser op eller han regner
            The wind is getting up, or it is raining.
          • 1915, Knut Hamsun, Segelfoss By‎, volume I, page 8:
            han er ikke vind
            There is no wind.
          • 1918, Gabriel Scott, Kilden‎, page 11:
            hvad slags veir er her idag, ja hvordan ser han igrunden ut – blaaser han tro, eller er han stille?
            What is the weather like here today, what is it really like—is it windy, I wonder, or is it calm?
          • 1926, Cora Sandel, Alberte og Jakob‎, page 235:
            under hende stimer og gaar sjøen med smaa, lette skvulp rundt stolpene. Han flør
            Below her the sea surges and laps gently around the posts. The tide is coming in.
          • 1949, Andreas Markusson, Gjennom brenningen‎, page 14:
            sjøl om han var bare storværet
            Even though the weather was stormy.
          • 1955, Liv Balstad, Nord for det øde hav‎, page 51:
            Han e’ tjukk i dag, ja!
            It is thick with fog today, yes!
          • 2002, Ragnhild Nilstun, For kjærlighets skyld‎:
            Han e svinkald
            It is bitterly cold.
        Usage notes
        • Han and ham are both standard object forms, including after prepositions; they have been equally accepted in Bokmål since 1938. Ham is not used as an ordinary subject.[1][2]
        • Han may resume or anticipate a noun phrase: Per, han kommer senere. ― Per, he will come later. Han kommer senere, Per. ― He will come later, Per.
        • Both han and ham occur in predicative expressions such as det er han/ham (“it is him”) and after comparisons such as eldre enn han/ham (“older than him”).
        • The possessive form is hans. When the pronoun refers back to the subject of the same clause, the reflexive forms seg and sin (si, sitt, sine) are normally used: Han så seg i speilet (“He saw himself in the mirror”), but Han så han i speilet (“He saw him in the mirror”).
        • Before names and kinship terms, unstressed han may be reduced to [n].
        • The pronoun normally has a lowercase initial, including when referring to God.[3]

        • hun (“she”), hen (“he/she”)

        Etymology 2

        Masculine nominalization of han (“he”, pronoun).

        Compare the parallel noun uses of Danish han (“male”), Swedish han (“male person”) and English he.

        Norwegian Nynorsk

        Etymology

        From Old Norse hann.

        Pronunciation

        • IPA(key): /hɑnː/

        Pronoun

        han

        1. he, him, it (third person singular, masculine)

        Usage notes

        Han is used to refer not only to masculine persons, but any masculine noun. E.g.: Bilen er fin. Eg likar han. - The car is nice. I like it.

        In some dialects, han may precede a male given name or a definite singular masculine noun. E.g: Kor vart det tå han Erik? (“Where did Erik disappeared?”)
